title: Dorayaki
subtitle: soft honey pancake sandwiches filled with red bean paste
excerpt: Dorayaki are two small, honey-flavoured Japanese pancakes sandwiched together with sweet red bean paste. They are soft, slightly springy, and one of Japan's most popular traditional sweets. Makes 12 dorayaki.
sourceNotes: Dorayaki is a traditional Japanese wagashi sweet that became widely popular in the twentieth century. It is named after the dora, a type of Japanese gong, which the pancakes resemble in shape.

recipe.freezeNotes: Wrap individually in cling film and freeze for up to 1 month. Defrost at room temperature for 30 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: The batter makes 24 small pancakes (enough for 12 dorayaki). Double for a larger batch.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The pancakes can be made a day ahead, wrapped in cling film, and filled just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: Japanese sweet red bean paste made from azuki beans and sugar. It is the traditional filling for wagashi and many Japanese sweets. Available as tsubu-an (chunky) or koshi-an (smooth).
Traditional Japanese confections, usually made with plant-based ingredients such as red beans, rice, and sugar. Dorayaki is a modern style of wagashi.

content.text: made from a honey-enriched pancake batter that produces a soft, slightly bouncy texture. The filling is
red bean paste, spread between two small pancakes and gently pressed together. Makes 12.
Resting the batter for 10 minutes after mixing is important. It lets the baking powder activate and relaxes the gluten so the pancakes cook flat with a fine, even bubble pattern on the surface.
Whisk the eggs, caster sugar, and brown sugar together in a bowl until pale and slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Add the sifted flour and baking powder to the egg mixture. Stir gently to combine. Add the water a little at a time and stir until you have a smooth, thick batter about the consistency of double cream. Rest for 10 minutes.
Heat the frying pan over medium-low heat. Wipe lightly with an oiled piece of kitchen paper. The pan should be just barely oiled, not greasy.

Drop 2 tablespoons of batter per pancake into the pan. Cook for 1 to 2 minutes until bubbles appear across the surface and the edges look set. Flip gently and cook for 30 seconds. Transfer to a clean cloth and cover to keep soft. Repeat until all the batter is used.

Match pancakes in pairs of similar size. Spread a generous tablespoon of red bean paste on the flat side of one pancake. Press the second pancake on top, flat-side down. Press gently to seal. Repeat with all the pairs.

attrs.cause: The sugar content makes them colour quickly when the pan is too hot.
attrs.fix: Cook over medium-low heat and wipe the pan clean between batches to remove burnt residue.

attrs.cause: The batter was overmixed or the pancakes were overcooked.
attrs.fix: Mix the batter until just combined and cover the cooked pancakes immediately with a damp cloth to keep them soft.

attrs.symptom: Filling is leaking out of the sides
attrs.cause: Too much paste was used or it was spread too close to the edges.
attrs.fix: Keep the paste at least 5 mm from the edge of the pancake and use a rounded tablespoon rather than a heaped one.

content.text: Dorayaki is sold in every Japanese convenience store, confectionery shop, and department store food hall. The sweet became globally famous as the favourite food of the cartoon character Doraemon. Despite that association, it is a serious traditional sweet with a long history. The honey-soft pancake and the sweet bean filling are a pairing that has not changed in decades because it does not need to.
